p:AFG: Da Afghanistan Bank is Afghanistan's central bank and issues the afghani. It scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side being corruption and secrecy around it, mainly corruption in the country, while the independence written into its law scores 0.87 of 1, where 1 means the bank holds the power. In May 2011 Afghanistan's High Office of Oversight and Anticorruption reported that the central bank had monitored Kabul Bank poorly; Kabul Bank had 925 million dollars in loans outstanding, many of them undocumented and given to powerful figures, before the central bank took it over in 2010. One career move is recorded, and a career move is not an accusation: Ajmal Ahmady came to the bank from money management, as a fixed income analyst at T. Rowe Price from 2008 to 2009, a sovereign analyst at Acadian Asset Management from 2009 to 2012 and in emerging market trading at Fortress Investment Group from 2012 to 2014, with a role at the emerging markets private equity group ACAP Partners, then government posts in Kabul, and was made acting governor by presidential decree in June 2020, serving until 15 August 2021. That dated career rests on Wikipedia, the only source that gives it; Harvard Kennedy School's own page for him, which is not Wikipedia, says that before his government work he held a variety of positions in the asset management industry and names Fortress Investment Group, Acadian Asset Management and T. Rowe Price. After the Taliban took power, the United States froze nearly 9.5 billion dollars of the bank's assets on 17 August 2021, much of it held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and stopped shipments of cash. On 11 February 2022 President Joe Biden signed an order splitting 7 billion dollars of the frozen money in two: 3.5 billion for relief in Afghanistan and 3.5 billion kept in the United States for lawsuits by US victims of terrorism. The bank holds 21.9 tonnes of gold, and its 2018 accounts were audited by Ernst & Young Ford Rhodes Sidat Hyder. A news report of 6 January 2020 said the bank had awarded the Polish Security Printing Works a contract for new 10, 20, 50 and 100 afghani notes, and on 1 February 2021 the Polish embassy in New Delhi announced that the works had delivered 380 million printed banknotes; no contract value is given and nothing says the arrangement continues.
p:BHS: The Central Bank of The Bahamas issues the Bahamian dollar, which as of December 2025 is held at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. Its board and its exchange rate policy are in the finance minister's hands by statute: under the Central Bank of The Bahamas Act 2020, published on 27 July 2020, the Governor, both Deputy Governors and six other directors are appointed by the Governor-General on the Minister's advice after consulting the Board, and a director or Deputy Governor is removed the same way, while section 5(1)(f) makes the bank advise the Minister on exchange rate policy and implement the policy the Minister determines. The Central Bank of The Bahamas (Amendment) Act, 2023 left those provisions alone, and the arrangement has no end date. In December 2022 the Bahamian government drew down 232.3 million dollars of special drawing rights, the reserve asset the International Monetary Fund issues to member countries, held through the central bank. The opposition's finance spokesman, Kwasi Thompson, said the advance was contrary to section 21 of the Central Bank Act, which sets limits on how much the bank may lend or advance to the government; that is his assertion, and no finding establishes a breach. What is on record as fact is what followed: the government tabled a bill stating that section 21 would not apply to the transaction, deemed to have come into force on 1 December 2022, and Governor John Rolle said in early January that a memorandum of understanding between the bank and the Ministry of Finance stipulated a change to the Central Bank Act. Two career moves are recorded, neither of them an accusation. T. Baswell Donaldson, who had managed the Bahamas Monetary Authority from 1968 and chaired it from 1972, was appointed the bank's first Governor and Board Chairman on 1 June 1974 and served until May 1980; afterwards he chaired the commercial bank Commonwealth Bank, whose ownership is not stated, as well as the Securities Commission and the College of The Bahamas Council, both public bodies, and was ambassador to the United States. James H. Smith was governor from 1987 to 1997 and chairs CFAL, which describes itself as a leading independent investment management and advisory firm based in Nassau and as the investment arm of Colina Holdings Ltd, the only statement of its ownership either page gives; his public roles include senator and minister of state in the Ministry of Finance from 2002 to 2007 and the chairmanship of the government-owned Bahamas Development Bank. The Bahamas scores 29 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed, its weak point secrecy: Bahamian law makes it hard to see who owns money there, scoring 75.4 of 100 for financial secrecy, ranked 32 of 141. No government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. Giesecke+Devrient printed the bank's new 1-dollar note, introduced on 3 February 2025, and the auditors' report in the 2011 annual report carries two signature blocks, Deloitte & Touche and BDO, each signed as Chartered Accountants at Nassau on 16 April 2012.
p:CUW: The Central Bank of Curacao and Sint Maarten issues the Caribbean guilder, pegged to the US dollar. It scores 50 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 96 per cent of the 194 places with a figure, its weakest side the local laws that hide who owns money, which score 78.2 of 100 for financial secrecy. Neither independence index codes it. Crane Currency, headquartered in Massachusetts with plants in Malta and Sweden and a supplier to more than 50 central banks, was contracted to print the new banknotes, with the Royal Canadian Mint making the coins. The bank's supervisory board came under pressure in May 2017. A report published on 26 May 2017 said the board had voted three to two to extend a managing director's term, short of the supermajority required, and that the finance minister, Richard Gibson, had written to the board members Robert Pietersz, Tom Kok, Miriela Carolina, Vance Williams and Hubert Lopez asking them to work on a solution; it quotes him saying that if a solution could not be found there would be no other choice but dismissal of the board, without naming who would carry it out. One case is recorded. In July 2024 a court found former president Tromp and former deputy director Laurents guilty of document forgery over a backdated 2009 loan agreement under which over 400,000 dollars went to Tromp's pension account. It acquitted them of official bribery and money laundering, including over a 1.5 million dollar payment in 2015 from the Venezuelan company Enpiso, which prosecutors linked to Girobank takeover talks. Two career moves are documented, and a career move is not an accusation. Bob Traa became president with effect from 13 June 2019 after working for the International Monetary Fund for over 34 years, a temporary appointment by the Supervisory Board pending official appointment by Curacao and Sint Maarten, with no private employer named. Jose Jardim, a board member and Financial Economic Director from 2017 responsible for financial and economic supervision and monetary policy, left on 30 June 2025 after eight years and became chief executive of Banco di Caribe, a commercial bank the central bank supervises, with effect from 1 July 2025; Banco di Caribe has been wholly owned since 2022 by United Group Holdings, a privately held group headed by the Curacao businessman Gregory Elias. The Supervisory Board's own announcement of his departure said only that he would take a leadership position at a commercial bank, without naming it.
p:DZA: The Bank of Algeria issues the dinar and holds it within a band of 2 per cent or less against the euro. Algeria scores 29 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, less exposed than 66 per cent of the 194 places with a figure, its weakest side corruption and secrecy around the bank, mainly laws that hide who owns money and money-laundering risk in its banks. Government pressure was reported in 3 of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, every time a demand to print money. One case is recorded, and it ended in acquittal: in the Khalifa Bank case the Blida criminal court sentenced former governor Abdelwahab Keramane in absentia to 20 years in prison in 2007, and on 7 June 2022 the same court acquitted him; the pages opened do not state the specific charges. On Monday 23 May 2022 Algeria's president Abdelmadjid Tebboune ended the duties of Rostom Fadhli as governor, with a statement from the presidency citing article 91 paragraph 7 and article 92 paragraph 7 of the constitution and giving no official reason; Fadhli had been appointed in June 2020 and had been expected to overhaul the 1990 money and credit law, a project that was not completed, and Salah Eddine Taleb, until then secretary of the Money and Credit Council, replaced him. One career move is on record, and it is not an accusation: Mohamed Lamine Lebbou, appointed governor in February 2026, began his career at BNP Paribas El Djazair from 2004 to 2006, a bank its own 2018 annual report says is 100 per cent owned by BNP Paribas France, and that is the private employer in his career; the banks he ran later are public, the state-owned Banque nationale d'Algerie from 2021 to 2024 and, from May 2025, BEA International Bank, the French subsidiary of the state Banque exterieure d'Algerie. The bank holds 173.6 tonnes of gold and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Who checks its books is a state body rather than a firm, and the arrangement sits close to having no outside auditor at all. Under the money and credit law of 21 June 2023, a Censorat of two full-time censeurs, appointed by presidential decree and required to have central bank accounting expertise, verifies the end-of-year accounts, reports to the bank's board and sends a report to the Minister of Finance within four months of the year end. The censeurs are put there by the head of state rather than chosen by the bank, and they answer to a minister; but the Censorat is created by the bank's own charter law and its members sit in its board sessions, which is why this is recorded with the doubt attached. No private firm is named anywhere in the law for the bank's own accounts.
p:LSO: Lesotho issues the loti, and the South African rand circulates alongside it. The Rand Monetary Area agreement was signed in December 1974 by South Africa, Swaziland and Lesotho, replaced by the Common Monetary Area in July 1986 and then by a Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992, when Namibia formally joined; member currencies are pegged to the rand at par and are legal tender only in the country that issues them, Lesotho must back what it issues fully with rand assets, and South Africa pays it an imputed return on rand circulating there as legal tender. All five of its current notes, introduced on 23 December 2021, are printed by De La Rue. In February 2024 three South Africans appeared in the Ficksburg Magistrates Court on fraud and money laundering charges over 57 million rand said to have been stolen from the Central Bank of Lesotho. The Hawks, a South African police unit, said Lesotho officials intercepted vouchers meant for service providers and diverted the payments to co-conspirators in South Africa, and that some officials were already before court in Lesotho. The charges are unproven. Two career moves are recorded, and neither is an accusation. Mr. O. 'Nete, a non-executive director on the bank's board, came from Standard Bank of Lesotho, where he was Senior Finance Manager, Finance Manager and Senior Manager Personal Credit, and earlier from Stanlib, where he was Tax Manager, with no dates given; Standard Bank Group's own structure page lists Standard Lesotho Bank Limited at 80 per cent among its holdings as at 30 June 2026, so that employer is majority owned by the Johannesburg-listed group rather than by the state. Mrs M. Mohasoa, also a non-executive director, was a board member and chairman of the audit and risk committee of the insurer Liberty Life Lesotho from 2017 to 2021, an insurer whose ownership is established through two further pages, the South African Reserve Bank's list of designated entities placing Liberty Life Lesotho Ltd within the Liberty Insurance Group and Liberty Holdings' own 2019 annual report stating that the stock-exchange-listed Standard Bank Group Limited holds 53.6 per cent of Liberty's issued ordinary share capital. Its 2023 accounts were audited by Moteane, Quashie & Associates with SizweNtsalubaGobodo Grant Thornton. Lesotho scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and corruption and secrecy around the bank is its weakest side, at 60. At a hearing on Monday 8 June 2026, at which the Auditor General presented consolidated financial statements for 31 March 2023 and 2024, the parliamentary Public Accounts Committee called for a forensic audit of the Central Bank of Lesotho to trace missing public money. Its chairperson, 'Machabana Lemphane-Letsie, said the bank must undergo a forensic audit and say who the money had been paid to. The figures in the report do not agree with each other: its headline puts the gap at M3.9 billion, while the statements it describes show government cash of M5.91 billion at 31 March 2024 against M2.82 billion in the consolidated accounts, a difference of M3.09 billion, which a quotation in the same piece also gives. The committee resolved that the Auditor General's office submit a budget for the audit by 30 June so it could go into the supplementary budget; that office said it has neither the expertise nor any budget allocated for one. The bank resisted, citing its own 2000 Act, which provides for an external auditor and limits the Auditor General to auditing currency balances rather than government payments the bank makes for the state.
p:MKD: North Macedonia's money is the denar, issued by the National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia and held in practice at a fixed rate to the euro. Its notes are printed abroad, by three firms in turn. The French firm Oberthur Fiduciaire was contracted for 100-denar notes, reported on 8 May 2026, for 59,800,000 denars, about 972,358 euros; the Russian joint-stock company Goznak had the 100-denar notes in 2021 for about 400,000 euros, part of a 2.2 million euro reissue carrying the state's changed constitutional name; and three contracts with De La Rue International cover the 10, 500 and 1,000 denar notes, 45 million notes for 3.775 million euros, 20 million of them polymer. The state's own auditors have gone through the bank's books once. The State Audit Office examined the bank's 2003 financial statements, working on site from 12 October to 20 December 2004 under article 2 of the Law on State Audit, and its final report, number 11-107/8 of 4 March 2005, carries a section headed improper and unlawful use of funds. It found that the National Bank had guaranteed a domestic bank with foreign-currency deposits, and that in January 2004 the foreign banks drew 20,759,515 US dollars from the National Bank's guarantee deposit. It also found that 30,210 thousand denars of purchases, 35.61 per cent of the purchases audited, were made without following the Public Procurement Law, and it told the bank to give up commercial activities that article 83 of the Law on the National Bank does not allow it. One case is recorded, running from 2017 to 2020, and it is unproven: an association of depositors of Eurostandard Bank said in a press release that the governor tipped off the finance minister and other large depositors so they could take their money out before the bank was put under administration, and that financial police reports were kept secret so it could keep operating. The association said Finance Minister Nina Angelovska withdrew more than 200,000 euros months before the central bank acted, and that over 60 million euros were lost; no charges and no official finding are reported. Two career moves are on record. Governor Anita Angelovska Bezhoska spent about eight years at the Ministry of Finance, ending as manager of the treasury department, was state secretary in 2003 and 2004, worked as an economist at the International Monetary Fund, and became governor in May 2018, a career with no private firm in it. Dimitar Bogov came from a commercial bank, as chief economist of Stopanska Banka AD Skopje, a member of the NBG Group, from 2002 to January 2007, then was vice governor and governor from 2011; no finding against him is reported. Grant Thornton DOO of Skopje signed the auditor's report on the 2023 accounts, with an opinion without qualifications, and the bank scores 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:NAM: The Bank of Namibia is the country's central bank. Namibia belongs to the Common Monetary Area with South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini, joining under the agreement of February 1992: the Namibian dollar is pegged to the South African rand one for one, and every Namibian dollar issued must be fully backed by rand assets. The bank scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side corruption and secrecy around it, and the law gives it middling independence, 0.637 of 1 and 103rd of 155 countries. In 2002 court papers in a suit by Nambib Resources against the Minister of Mines listed governor Tom Alweendo as a 10 per cent shareholder in Trade Line Namibia, which held an exclusive licence to prospect on the Skeleton Coast. Alweendo said he had been made a director without his knowledge, and no finding or outcome is reported, so the allegation is unproven. Johannes !Gawaxab came from a private-sector banking career to the governorship on 1 June 2020, succeeding Ipumbu Shiimi; the headline of the article is the only place that describes him as coming from the private sector, and no firm, role or dates are named, and the bank's board page now shows Ebson Uanguta as governor from 1 January 2026. On 13 April 2026, in the question-and-answer session after her State of the Nation Address, President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah said the reported losses at the Bank of Namibia, together with missing Government Institutions Pension Fund money, were smelling of corruption and must be investigated. Affirmative Repositioning leader Job Amupanda said the central bank had made a loss close to a billion dollars for unexplained reasons. No investigation is reported as having been ordered, and no body is named as the one that would carry it out. Deloitte Namibia and Grand Namibia audit its accounts, and De La Rue printed its new 50-dollar note.
p:WSM: The Central Bank of Samoa issues the Samoan currency, which as of December 2025 is kept within a crawling band of 2 per cent or less measured against the US and Australian dollars. Samoa scores 32 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 52 per cent of the 194 places with a figure. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around the bank, mainly because the country's laws hide who owns money and because of money-laundering risk in its banks. One finding is on record: a performance audit of government debt servicing carried out by the Samoa Audit Office in 2014 compared the due dates of government debt repayments with the dates the Central Bank of Samoa actually made them and found instances where repayments had been delayed. The same audit recorded that there was no formalised arrangement between the Ministry of Finance and the central bank, and its recommendations went to the Ministry of Finance, including that the two bodies formalise their responsibilities; no wrongdoing by any person is alleged in it. In April 2026 the government pressed ahead with changes to the bank's own law that would widen the Finance Minister's role and move some of the bank's rules into regulations. In a letter to the Attorney-General's office the bank said the changes had come as a surprise and warned they could weaken its independence, increase political influence and create legal uncertainty. The International Monetary Fund wrote to Finance Minister Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molio'o on 9 April 2026 warning that the reforms could weaken the bank's autonomy, and Prime Minister Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Polataivao Schmidt rejected the warnings as outside interference. The bank was created in 1984, and its law has been changed three times since 1970, each change giving it more independence. Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank, and BDO Chartered Accountants audited the financial statements for the year ended 30 June 2025.
p:TJK: The National Bank of Tajikistan issues the somoni, which it keeps within a band of 2 per cent or less against the US dollar. The Law on the National Bank of Tajikistan, No. 722 of 28 June 2011, signed by President Emomali Rahmon, puts every seat on the bank's Board in the President's hands. Article 74(4) has the Chairman and his deputies appointed and released from office by presidential decree, with the decrees submitted to the lower house of parliament for approval; article 74(3) has the Board's three independent members approved by the President on the Chairman's proposal; and article 74(6) has the President set the salary of the Chairman and his deputies. One case is recorded, as an official finding: in March 2008 the International Monetary Fund's Executive Board found the bank had supplied inaccurate information on the cotton sector, international reserves, net domestic assets and credit policy, reporting reserves of about 450 million US dollars when they were roughly a third of that and concealing that reserves were pledged as collateral for cotton loans; Tajikistan was required to repay 47.4 million US dollars. No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. Four career moves run in the same direction, all of them to one commercial bank, Spitamen Bank, whose charter names a single shareholder, the limited liability insurance and reinsurance company Spitamen Insurance, and calls the bank a commercial organisation; none of the four is an accusation. Navruz Samandarzoda, who had headed the bank's research and modelling department, joined Spitamen Bank in January 2018 and chairs its Management Board; Mahmud Hamralizoda, a leading specialist and then deputy head of the central bank's international relations department from 2018 to 2021, joined its Supervisory Board in January 2023; Sanovbar Dzhabirova, at the central bank from 1996 to 2008 and again from 2016 to 2021, latterly as head and then deputy director of its accounting department, joined the same Supervisory Board in January 2023; and Dilbar Khuseynova, head of the insurance control department from 2017 to 2024, joined it in October 2024, having worked at the Development Bank of Tajikistan and at Spitamen Bank itself before her years at the central bank as well as after. It has one swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency: 3 billion yuan with China, signed on 3 September 2015 to run three years and extendable by agreement, drawn on for 1 million yuan in January 2016; whether it is in force is not known. Its commemorative 100-somoni note, circulated on 30 October 2025, was printed by Giesecke+Devrient of Germany, that note alone and not the regular series. RSM Tajikistan LLC signed the auditor's report on the 2023 statements; the firm holds a licence to audit banks issued by the National Bank itself, so the body being audited also licenses its auditor. Earlier audits were done by Deloitte and by Ernst & Young Ford Rhodes Sidat Hyder. Tajikistan scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed.
p:DOM: The Dominican Republic's money is the peso, issued by the Central Bank of the Dominican Republic and held within a crawling band of 2 per cent or less against the US dollar as of December 2025. The bank scores 22 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, less exposed than 93 per cent of the 194 places with a figure. On a date the source does not give, the Directorate for the Prosecution of Administrative Corruption took former governor Jose Lois Malkun, former deputy governor Felix Calvo, former administrative director Cesar Apolinar Veloz and former legal counsel Manuel Rubio Cristoforis to court on charges including breach of trust and criminal association, over 18 missing promissory notes worth 10,663 million Dominican pesos said to have been handed fraudulently to the former banker Manuel Arturo Pellerano. Those charges are unproven. The bank neither complained nor joined the case, and a Monetary Board resolution signed by legal counsel Olga Morel said its authorities were negotiating the notes' return with Pellerano. One career move is recorded, and it is a move between public bodies rather than an accusation: George Manuel Hazoury sat on the Monetary Board, the bank's governing board, after serving as administrator of Banco de Reservas, which is the Dominican state's own bank, and he left the board in 2020 when decree 532-20 named the economists Arturo Martinez Moya and Eduardo Tejera to it for two years, alongside the departure of Manuel Garcia Arevalo, a former Minister of Industry and Commerce. The Polish Security Printing Works says it produced 55 million banknotes for the Dominican Republic in 2018, naming no counterparty and no contract value, and adds that most of its contracts are secret. KPMG audited the financial statements as at 31 December 2023.
p:BTN: Bhutan's central bank is the Royal Monetary Authority, which issues the ngultrum and keeps it pegged, or fixed, to the Indian rupee; the rupee circulates in the country as well. Its own law lets the government direct it: under the Royal Monetary Authority Act of Bhutan 2010, passed on 2 June 2010 and in force from 22 June 2010, section 149 lets the Royal Government issue such directives to the Authority as it considers necessary in the public interest, after consulting the Governor and reporting them to Parliament. Four of the Board's seven members are appointed by the Government, one of them from the Ministry of Finance, and the Royal Government sets the Governor's salary and the board members' fees. The Governor is appointed by the Druk Gyalpo on the Prime Minister's recommendation and may be removed the same way, but only on a committee finding of permanent incapacity, incapability of carrying out the duties or breach of the code of conduct. The Act repealed the 1982 Royal Monetary Authority Act, and the arrangement is standing, with no end date. An anonymous informer raised a case in October 2014, and the final findings of Bhutan's Anti-Corruption Commission, covering 2014 to 2016, said a former deputy governor had allegedly forged official documents, misused power and concealed earnings from World Bank and Asian Development Bank projects. Those allegations are unproven; the case was forwarded to the Office of the Attorney General, with no later outcome. Two career moves are recorded, and every post in them is a public one. Dasho Penjore began at the Royal Monetary Authority in 1987, was its Deputy Managing Director from 2003 to 2006, was appointed Chief Chamberlain to the King in 2006, was Chief Executive Officer of the National Pension and Provident Fund of Bhutan, a statutory pension body, and was appointed Governor of the Authority in December 2015. Damche Tenzin was Chief Legal Advisor and Company Secretary and then Chief Support Officer of Bank of Bhutan Limited from September 2008 to December 2014, then Chief General Counsel of the National Pension and Provident Fund until May 2016, and has been Chief General Counsel of the Royal Monetary Authority since 1 June 2016; Bank of Bhutan is 80 per cent owned by Druk Holding & Investments, a holding company owned by the government of Bhutan, with 20 per cent held by the State Bank of India, so that side of the move is public too. A commemorative 1,000-ngultrum note marking the Fourth King's seventieth birth anniversary was printed by De La Rue, and M/s P.K. Mitra & Company audited the accounts for 2003 and 2004. India opened a swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency, of up to 100 million US dollars or its equivalent on 17 March 2016 under the Reserve Bank of India's SAARC framework; its three-year term ran out in March 2019. The bank scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:TLS: Timor-Leste has its own central bank, the Central Bank of Timor-Leste, created in 2001, but not its own currency: it uses the United States dollar. The International Monetary Fund's 2023 classification lists it among the places with no separate legal tender and the dollar as anchor. One case is recorded. In its report and opinion on the 2019 General State Account, the country's Court of Accounts found that 6.6 million US dollars of European Union direct budget support, held in three bank accounts at the central bank, was not booked as state revenue, so 2019 state revenue was understated by that amount, and that the 2.3 million US dollars spent from those accounts was spent outside the state budget and the General State Account. The same report recorded a closing accounting balance of 4.4 million US dollars against a cash balance at the central bank of 5.2 million. One career move is recorded, and every employer in it is a public or multilateral body: Helder Lopes, governor from 2023 to 2029, had been Minister of Finance and Vice Minister of Finance, an adviser to the President and to the Ministry of Finance, and earlier a senior economist on the Asian Development Bank's private sector development initiative in Timor-Leste. Timor-Leste scores 34 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 64 per cent of the 194 places with a figure. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, 57, with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 44 of 100 for 2025. The independence the law gives the bank is comparatively strong, 0.777 of 1 and rank 50 of 191. Ernst & Young Audit & Associados - SROC, S.A. audited the 2023 accounts.
